title: Kimetsu no Yaiba Movie 1: Mugenjou-hen - Akaza Sairai
content:
When words have first spread around that Demon Slayer would be adapting more of its arcs into movies instead of serialized seasonal releases, you can’t imagine how toxic and controversial it got to start a DS discussion. Fans were in shambles, the Mugen train arc was a resonance signal to the anime industry that theatrical releases for adapting canons material are huge money makers. And as you’d imagine, investors were not about to let that one pass.

Love it or hate it, the Mugen train was a marvel in terms of optimizing pacing for a canon arc adaptation. And the first Infinity Castle arc movie tookthat to new highs.

Pacing being one of the most commonly complained about aspects of a given show, this movie leaves no room for that. From start to finish, all scenes transition seamlessly with no awkward moments of silence or stretched up exchanges. The balance between action, comedy and emotional moments is a feat in and of its own. Never has a dialogue felt like it went on for more than it was welcomed for, nor has a fight continued for longer than what your attention span required. It was a gripping, suspenseful full on assault that takes place at and uncharted territory, where stakes were higher than ever, stakes that left lasting damage and losses on both sides.

Another aspect, or rather, criticism, that’s popular to hear within the Demon Slayer circles is how average and stereotypical all the characters are. I mean, it’s only normal that a Shounen series would show its shortcomings time to time, I mean, we have basically come to memorize the whole blueprint by now. The same goes for all other genres, but I’ll give credit to this movie for at least flashily and carefully spotlighting the right amount of characters during the right moments. It was laid out in a way that the narrative sort of paid respect to every passing or grieving character, writing them a beautiful farewell poem despite their alignment. Once again, the backstories strike the same mundane vibes that sit you back and leave you pondering, all of these characters having very normal relatable pasts once removed from the under the whole supernatural veil.

I was gonna spare us from the usual animation glaze, seeing as it is Ufotable we’re talking about, however, this movie capitalizes on that and pulls no punches, a fitting for display for Akaza himself.

Many Manga fans were worried that the whole deal with the complex and seemingly infinite location the arc takes place in, the Infinity Castle, the production was going to cheap out on  environmental design or fallback to poorly rendered CG scenes. But no, the talent at Ufotable came up with one of the strongest modern arguments in favor of CG use in animation production.

The blend between the 2D, sometimes rotoscoped animations, with the dynamic, ever extending background and environments, coupled with the seamless presence of layered visual effects and particles resulted in an ocular wonder the likes of which is very addicting. Wallpapers at every frame kinda of quality.

I could go on and on, but let me stop there or else I’d be doing the sound design and voice acting a disfavor. it would have been a shame if all of that eye feast slipped by with no audible masterclass to rival. And I say rival because the latter was strong enough to stand on its on.

Retrospectively, I feel like these theatrical releases pave the way for the series to be more binge friendly and future proof. The movie formal in general is more accessible and does not gate keep the story behind tons of episodes and seasons.

Overall: 8.46/10.
